opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because there are many people working on alignment in different places: academia, nonprofits, other labs. The question is what we can do that others can't, or can't do as well.

The most obvious thing is that we have access to the most capable models, often before anyone else, and we can train our own. That matters a lot. Much alignment research only becomes meaningful at the frontier. Some techniques that work on small models just break, and some problems don't show up until models are capable enough. If you want to know whether something like RLHF or scalable oversight actually works, you have to try it on the systems people will actually deploy. Academics mostly can't do that, so it would be a waste for us to focus on things that could just as well be done on GPT-2-sized models in a university lab.

The second advantage is compute and engineering. A lot of the most promising alignment work looks like engineering more than theory: building training pipelines, running large experiments, setting up evaluations that need many forward passes. We're well positioned for empirical work at scale, so I've tried to steer the team toward that rather than very theoretical, pen-and-paper agendas. Those agendas are valuable, but others can pursue them.

Third, we're close to deployment. We see how models behave with real users, where they fail, and what people try to make them do. That's a feedback loop most researchers don't have. It keeps the research grounded in real problems, and it means our alignment techniques can actually ship and influence what millions of people use.

The fourth one I'd stress is that we can use the models themselves to do alignment research. That's central to how I think about the whole problem. The long-term bet is that we build AI systems that help us evaluate other AI systems, help us find flaws, and eventually help with alignment research directly. Being at a lab training these models makes it much easier to pursue that seriously and to iterate quickly as capabilities improve.

There are trade-offs, of course. Being inside a lab brings commercial pressures, and you have to keep focused on the hard, long-term problems rather than only today's product issues. But overall, I think the right strategy is to lean into what's unique about being here: frontier models, scale, deployment experience, and the chance to bootstrap alignment research with the systems we're building. We should leave other kinds of work to the many good people elsewhere who are better placed to do it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually a really important question, and it's something we've thought about a lot when deciding what the team should focus on.

So the obvious thing is that we have access to the frontier models. We can study them, we can fine-tune them, we can run experiments on them at scale. And a lot of alignment research, especially the more empirical kind, really benefits from that. If you want to know how a technique behaves on the most capable system that exists, you have to have the most capable system. That's not something most academic labs can do, and I think it would be a mistake for us not to lean into it.

The second thing is compute. Some of the experiments we want to run are expensive. Training reward models, doing lots of RL from human feedback runs, scaling up interpretability methods to large models. We're in a position where we can actually do those, so we should prioritize the research that requires that kind of scale, rather than things that a small group with a few GPUs could do just as well.

And the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that we're embedded in an organization that's actually deploying these systems. So we get feedback from the real world. We see where models fail, where users push on them, where the alignment techniques break down in practice. That's a very different signal from what you get working purely in theory. It keeps us honest about what the actual problems are.

So putting those together, my view is our comparative advantage is in empirical alignment work on frontier systems. That means things like RLHF and its successors, scalable oversight, using AI to help evaluate AI, and generally trying to build alignment techniques that we can actually test today and iterate on. It doesn't mean the more theoretical or conceptual work isn't valuable. It's just that other people are better positioned to do it, and I'd rather we do the thing only we can do.

The flip side is that we have to be careful about the incentives. Being inside a lab that's racing to build more capable systems creates some pressure, and I think we have a responsibility to use our position to actually push on the hard problems, not just the ones that make the product better. That's something I think about a lot.

astra-6.text:
I think we should focus on work that really benefits from being at OpenAI. We have access to capable models, the infrastructure to train them, and people who know a lot about how to make that work. So we can test alignment ideas at a scale that would be difficult for most academic groups to do.

That pushes us toward an empirical approach: take an alignment method, try it on the best models we have, and study where it breaks. Can humans reliably evaluate what the model is doing? Can we use AI assistance to make that evaluation better? And as models become more capable, do our methods keep working?

There’s also a lot of value in working closely with the people building and deploying the models. You get feedback about which problems actually arise, and there’s a path for research results to become part of the training process.

That doesn’t mean theoretical work isn’t important. It means that, when we choose between projects, we should ask: is this something we’re particularly well placed to do? If a project could be done just as well by a small group without access to large models, there’s less reason for it to be our main focus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main comparative advantage is that we have access to the models that we’re trying to align, and we work closely with the people who train them. So we should really make use of that. We can study alignment problems in the most capable systems we have, try out techniques, and get feedback about what actually works.

That pushes us towards a fairly empirical approach. Rather than trying to solve the whole problem in the abstract, we can ask: where do our current methods break down? What happens when the model becomes more capable? Can we get it to help us evaluate outputs that are difficult for humans to judge?

And then there’s a close connection to deployment. If we develop something useful, there’s a path to putting it into the systems that people actually use. That also gives us feedback on whether we’re solving the right problems. I think we should focus on work where those advantages really matter, while recognising that other groups can pursue approaches that don’t depend on having access to frontier models.
